Jacqueline Friedland's *Estimating Unpaid Claims Using Basic Techniques*
(Casualty Actuarial Society, version 3, 2010) is the CAS syllabus text on
reserving. It applies each technique to the same few data sets, so the results
of one chapter feed the next: the development factors of chapter 7 become the
reporting pattern of chapters 9 and 10, and the expected claims of chapter 8 the
prior of chapter 9. This guide follows that path in prospicio with the book's
own data, and prints the book's printed figures next to prospicio's.

This is the R twin of the Python guide
[`reserving-friedland.md`](reserving-friedland.md): the same sections, data and
numbers. The R package calls the same Rust code as the Python one, so every
figure below equals the Python guide's.

The text and exhibits are Friedland's; what follows explains them in new words
and recomputes the numbers. Exhibit numbers are the book's, and they restart in
every chapter, so "Exhibit II" always comes with its chapter. Money is in
thousands of dollars, as in the exhibits. For the choice between methods on your
own data, read [`reserving-methods.md`](reserving-methods.md).

Each R chunk is followed by the text it prints.
`R/prospicio/tests/test-guides.R` runs the chunks in order and requires each
one to print exactly that text. To render the page, install the R package
(`remotes::install_github`, see `R/prospicio/bootstrap.R`) and run
`quarto render docs/guides/reserving-friedland.qmd`.

## 1. The two data sets

The book's chapters 7 to 10 work through two examples.

- **U.S. Industry Auto**: reported and paid claims of the whole U.S. private
  passenger auto industry, accident years 1998 to 2007, valued at December 31,
  2007, with earned premium. Large and stable: every method should agree.
- **XYZ Insurer, Auto BI**: a small insurer's bodily injury book, accident
  years 1998 to 2008, valued at December 31, 2008. Its case reserving, its
  settlement speed and a tort reform all changed, so the methods disagree.
  Only calendar years 2000 to 2008 exist, so the two oldest rows start at 36
  and 24 months.

The triangles are typed from chapter 7, Exhibits I and II (sheets 1 and 2),
and the premiums from chapter 8, Exhibits II and III:

```{r}

# A triangle from rows of cumulative values; exposures are repeated on every
# cell. With `diagonals = n`, only the latest n calendar diagonals are kept.
make_triangle <- function(years, columns, exposures = list(),
                          first_age = rep(12, length(years)), diagonals = NULL) {
  rows <- columns[[1]]
  long <- NULL
  for (i in seq_along(years)) {
    for (k in seq_along(rows[[i]])) {
      months <- first_age[i] + 12 * (k - 1)
      if (!is.null(diagonals) && years[i] + months %/% 12 - 1 <= max(years) - diagonals) next
      cell <- data.frame(origin = years[i], age = months)
      for (name in names(columns)) cell[[name]] <- columns[[name]][[i]][k]
      for (name in names(exposures)) cell[[name]] <- exposures[[name]][i]
      long <- rbind(long, cell)
    }
  }
  triangle(long, "origin", "age", c(names(columns), names(exposures)))
}

us <- make_triangle(US_YEARS, list(reported = US_REPORTED, paid = US_PAID),
                    list(premium = US_PREMIUM))
xyz <- make_triangle(XYZ_YEARS, list(reported = XYZ_REPORTED, paid = XYZ_PAID),
                     list(premium = XYZ_PREMIUM), first_age = XYZ_FIRST_AGE)
latest <- function(tri, column) latest_diagonal(tri)[1, column, ]
cat("U.S. latest: reported", comma(sum(latest(us, "reported"))), "paid", comma(sum(latest(us, "paid"))),
    "premium", comma(sum(latest(us, "premium"))), "\n")
print(xyz@values[1, "reported", 1:3, 1:5])
```

The XYZ rows for 1998 and 1999 begin with unobserved cells (`NA`). prospicio
keeps them as missing, not zero, so they take no part in any factor.

## 2. The development technique (chapter 7)

### Age-to-age factors and their averages

Friedland's averages of the link ratios run over the **latest** few accident
years: simple averages of the latest 5 and 3, a medial average of the latest 5
without the highest and lowest, volume-weighted averages of the latest 5 and 3,
and a geometric average of the latest 4. `chain_ladder()` averages all years
(`average = "volume"`, `"simple"` or `"regression"`) and has no option for the
latest n years or for medial and geometric averages, so the helper computes
them from `link_ratios()` and the cells:

```{r}
#| label: averages
links <- function(tri, column) {
  lr <- link_ratios(tri)@values[1, column, , , drop = FALSE][1, 1, , ]
  lapply(seq_len(ncol(lr)), function(k) lr[!is.na(lr[, k]), k])
}

averages <- function(tri, column) {
  cells <- tri@values[1, column, , ]
  volume <- function(k, n) {
    ok <- which(!is.na(cells[, k + 1]))
    ok <- tail(ok, n)
    sum(cells[ok, k + 1]) / sum(cells[ok, k])
  }
  medial <- function(x) {
    x <- sort(tail(x, 5))
    if (length(x) > 2) mean(x[2:(length(x) - 1)]) else mean(x)
  }
  lr <- links(tri, column)
  ks <- seq_along(lr)
  list(
    "simple, latest 5" = sapply(lr, function(x) mean(tail(x, 5))),
    "simple, latest 3" = sapply(lr, function(x) mean(tail(x, 3))),
    "medial, latest 5x1" = sapply(lr, medial),
    "volume, latest 5" = sapply(ks, volume, n = 5),
    "volume, latest 3" = sapply(ks, volume, n = 3),
    "geometric, latest 4" = sapply(lr, function(x) exp(mean(log(tail(x, 4)))))
  )
}

av <- averages(us, "reported")
for (name in names(av)) cat(sprintf("%-20s", name), f3(av[[name]]), "\n")
```

```text
simple, latest 5     1.168 1.058 1.027 1.011 1.004 1.003 1.002 1.001 1.000
simple, latest 3     1.164 1.056 1.027 1.012 1.005 1.003 1.002 1.001 1.000
medial, latest 5x1   1.165 1.057 1.027 1.010 1.004 1.003 1.002 1.001 1.000
volume, latest 5     1.168 1.058 1.027 1.011 1.004 1.003 1.002 1.001 1.000
volume, latest 3     1.164 1.056 1.027 1.012 1.005 1.003 1.002 1.001 1.000
geometric, latest 4  1.164 1.057 1.027 1.011 1.004 1.003 1.002 1.001 1.000
```

Each row equals the corresponding row of chapter 7, Exhibit I, sheet 1, part 3,
to the three decimals printed (12-24 at the left); the paid averages on sheet 2
agree in the same way. The book's medial average of two values is their simple
average and of one value the value itself, as the helper does.

A volume-weighted average over the latest n years also comes out of prospicio
itself: keep the latest `n + 1` calendar diagonals and fit the ordinary
volume-weighted chain ladder. The all-year averages are not what the book uses:

```{r}
#| label: recent
recent <- make_triangle(US_YEARS, list(reported = US_REPORTED), diagonals = 4)
cat("volume, latest 3 ", f3(chain_ladder(recent, "reported")@ldf), "\n")
cat("volume, all years", f3(chain_ladder(us, "reported")@ldf), "\n")
cat("simple, all years", f3(chain_ladder(us, "reported", average = "simple")@ldf), "\n")
```

```text
volume, latest 3  1.164 1.056 1.027 1.012 1.005 1.003 1.002 1.001 1.000
volume, all years 1.175 1.058 1.027 1.011 1.004 1.003 1.002 1.001 1.000
simple, all years 1.175 1.058 1.027 1.011 1.004 1.003 1.002 1.001 1.000
```

The all-year factors at 12-24 (1.175) are well above the book's selection of
1.164, because the early accident years developed more in their first year.

### Selected factors, factors to ultimate, and rounding

For U.S. Industry Auto, Friedland selects the latest-3 averages, rounded to
three decimals, with no tail for reported claims and a tail of 1.002 for paid.
She rounds the factors to ultimate (CDF) to three decimals again before
multiplying them into the latest diagonal. Selected factors go in with `ldf`
(a vector named by age) and `ldf_kind = "ldf"`, a constant tail with `tail`:

```{r}
#| label: selected
AGES <- us@development
SEL_REPORTED <- c(1.164, 1.056, 1.027, 1.012, 1.005, 1.003, 1.002, 1.001, 1.000)
SEL_PAID <- c(1.702, 1.186, 1.091, 1.044, 1.019, 1.009, 1.005, 1.002, 1.002)
named <- function(values, ages = AGES) stats::setNames(values, ages[seq_along(values)])
dev_r <- chain_ladder(us, "reported", ldf = named(SEL_REPORTED), ldf_kind = "ldf")
dev_p <- chain_ladder(us, "paid", ldf = named(SEL_PAID), ldf_kind = "ldf", tail = 1.002)
cat("reported CDF", sprintf("%.5f", dev_r@cdf), "\n")
cat("paid CDF    ", sprintf("%.5f", dev_p@cdf), "\n")
cat("total ultimate: reported", comma(sum(dev_r@ultimate)), "(book 569,172,456)\n")
cat("                paid    ", comma(sum(dev_p@ultimate)), "(book 572,041,099)\n")
```

```text
reported CDF 1.29163 1.10964 1.05080 1.02317 1.01104 1.00601 1.00300 1.00100 1.00000 1.00000
paid CDF     2.39003 1.40425 1.18402 1.08526 1.03952 1.02014 1.01104 1.00601 1.00400 1.00200
total ultimate: reported 569,136,323 (book 569,172,456)
                paid     572,052,982 (book 572,041,099)
```

The totals miss the book by 36,133 and 11,883 (thousands): the product of the
reported factors from 12 months is 1.29163, which the book uses as 1.292. Give
the book's rounded CDFs as the pattern with `ldf_kind = "cdf"`; a pattern given
to the oldest age with no `tail` keeps its last value as the tail:

```{r}
#| label: rounded
CDF_REPORTED <- c(1.292, 1.110, 1.051, 1.023, 1.011, 1.006, 1.003, 1.001, 1.000, 1.000)
CDF_PAID <- c(2.390, 1.404, 1.184, 1.085, 1.040, 1.020, 1.011, 1.006, 1.004, 1.002)
US_CDF <- list(reported = named(CDF_REPORTED), paid = named(CDF_PAID))
dev_r <- chain_ladder(us, "reported", ldf = US_CDF$reported, ldf_kind = "cdf")
dev_p <- chain_ladder(us, "paid", ldf = US_CDF$paid, ldf_kind = "cdf")
cat("paid tail", dev_p@pattern_tail, "\n")

BOOK_DEV <- list(  # chapter 7, Exhibit I, sheet 3, columns (7) and (8)
  reported = c(47742304, 51185767, 54892767, 56468461, 58944268,
               58198563, 58287120, 59682517, 60651886, 63118803),
  paid = c(47739475, 51204536, 54860424, 56493084, 58963359,
           58167880, 58345519, 59963673, 61223522, 65079626)
)
cat(sprintf("%4s %12s %12s %12s %12s\n", "year", "reported", "book", "paid", "book"))
for (i in seq_along(US_YEARS)) {
  cat(sprintf("%4d %s %s %s %s\n", US_YEARS[i], comma(dev_r@ultimate[i], 12), comma(BOOK_DEV$reported[i], 12),
              comma(dev_p@ultimate[i], 12), comma(BOOK_DEV$paid[i], 12)))
}
cat(sprintf("%4s %s %s %s %s\n", "all", comma(sum(dev_r@ultimate), 12), comma(569172456, 12),
            comma(sum(dev_p@ultimate), 12), comma(572041099, 12)))
```

Every ultimate now equals sheet 3. IBNR is ultimate less reported and the
total unpaid ultimate less paid (the book's sheet 4); prospicio's `reserve` is
ultimate less the column's latest value, so on the paid triangle it is the
total unpaid:

```{r}
#| label: unpaid
unpaid <- function(ultimate, tri = us) {
  c(sum(ultimate) - sum(latest(tri, "reported")), sum(ultimate) - sum(latest(tri, "paid")))
}
show_unpaid <- function(name, ultimate, book, tri = us, width = 11) {
  u <- unpaid(ultimate, tri)
  cat(sprintf("%-8s IBNR %s (book %s)  total unpaid %s (book %s)\n", name, comma(u[1], width),
              comma(book[1], width), comma(u[2], width), comma(book[2], width)))
}
show_unpaid("reported", dev_r@ultimate, c(25690869, 71122088))
show_unpaid("paid", dev_p@ultimate, c(28559512, 73990731))
cat("paid reserve = total unpaid:", comma(dev_p@total_reserve), "\n")
```

```text
reported IBNR  25,690,869 (book  25,690,869)  total unpaid  71,122,088 (book  71,122,088)
paid     IBNR  28,559,512 (book  28,559,512)  total unpaid  73,990,731 (book  73,990,731)
paid reserve = total unpaid: 73,990,731
```

### The tail factor

Friedland's paid tail of 1.002 is a judgment set beside the reported pattern,
which has reached 1.000 at 120 months. A fitted exponential curve gives a factor
close to hers:

```{r}
#| label: tail
curve <- chain_ladder(us, "paid", tail = tail_curve())
cat(sprintf("fitted tail %.4f, book's selection 1.002\n", curve@tail))
```

```text
fitted tail 1.0011, book's selection 1.002
```

### XYZ Insurer: unstable factors and a pattern below 1

For XYZ, Friedland selects the volume-weighted average of the latest 2 years at
every age, with no reported tail and a paid tail of 1.010. The latest 3
diagonals reproduce her selected factors (chapter 7, Exhibit II, sheets 1 and
2, part 4):

```{r}
#| label: xyz-factors
for (column in c("reported", "paid")) {
  rows <- if (column == "reported") XYZ_REPORTED else XYZ_PAID
  last2 <- make_triangle(XYZ_YEARS, stats::setNames(list(rows), column),
                         first_age = XYZ_FIRST_AGE, diagonals = 3)
  cat(sprintf("%-8s", column), f3(chain_ladder(last2, column)@ldf), "\n")
}
```

```text
reported 1.687 1.265 1.102 1.020 1.050 1.010 1.011 1.000 0.993 0.999
paid     3.349 2.079 1.574 1.316 1.203 1.136 1.059 1.022 1.017 1.004
```

The book prints the same factors. Its reported CDFs at 96 and 108 months are
0.992, below 1, which `ldf_kind = "cdf"` refuses, so they go in as ratios of
consecutive CDFs with `ldf_kind = "ldf"`; the paid CDFs go in directly:

```{r}
#| label: xyz-dev
XYZ_AGES <- xyz@development
CDF_XYZ_REPORTED <- c(2.551, 1.512, 1.196, 1.085, 1.064, 1.013, 1.003, 0.992, 0.992, 0.999, 1.000)
CDF_XYZ_PAID <- c(21.999, 6.569, 3.160, 2.007, 1.525, 1.268, 1.116, 1.054, 1.031, 1.014, 1.010)
n <- length(XYZ_AGES)
ratios <- named(CDF_XYZ_REPORTED[-n] / CDF_XYZ_REPORTED[-1], XYZ_AGES)
xdev_r <- chain_ladder(xyz, "reported", ldf = ratios, ldf_kind = "ldf")
xdev_p <- chain_ladder(xyz, "paid", ldf = named(CDF_XYZ_PAID, XYZ_AGES), ldf_kind = "cdf")

BOOK_XDEV <- list(  # chapter 7, Exhibit II, sheet 3, columns (7) and (8)
  reported = c(15822, 25082, 36948, 38487, 48313, 44950, 74787, 76661, 58370, 47979, 47530),
  paid = c(15980, 25164, 37922, 40600, 49592, 49858, 80537, 80333, 72108, 77941, 74995)
)

# prospicio's ultimates beside the book's; columns: name -> list(ultimates, book, book total).
compare <- function(years, columns, width = 8) {
  cat("year", paste(sprintf("%*s %*s", width, names(columns), width, "book"), collapse = " "), "\n")
  for (i in seq_along(years)) {
    cells <- vapply(columns, function(c) paste(comma(c[[1]][i], width), comma(c[[2]][i], width)), "")
    cat(sprintf("%4d", years[i]), paste(cells, collapse = " "), "\n")
  }
  cells <- vapply(columns, function(c) paste(comma(sum(c[[1]]), width), comma(c[[3]], width)), "")
  cat(" all", paste(cells, collapse = " "), "\n")
}

compare(XYZ_YEARS, list(reported = list(xdev_r@ultimate, BOOK_XDEV$reported, 514929),
                        paid = list(xdev_p@ultimate, BOOK_XDEV$paid, 605030)))
```

The reported total equals the book's 514,929 and the paid total is 2 below
605,030; single years differ by 1 in both directions. The book's spreadsheet
holds claims with decimals and prints them in whole thousands: 38,798 times
0.992 is 38,487.6, but a latest value of 38,797.5 (printed 38,798) gives the
book's 38,487. Section 3 shows the same effect in a printed column total.

## 3. The expected claims technique (chapter 8)

Ultimate is an expected claim ratio times earned premium. For U.S. Industry
Auto the book selects 75% for 1998 to 2002 and 65% for 2003 to 2007 (chapter 8,
Exhibit II, sheet 1). With a ratio by year, put the expected claims in a column
and fit with `apriori = 1`:

```{r}
#| label: ec
US_RATIO <- c(rep(0.75, 5), rep(0.65, 5))
us <- make_triangle(US_YEARS, list(reported = US_REPORTED, paid = US_PAID),
                    list(premium = US_PREMIUM, expected = US_RATIO * US_PREMIUM))
ec <- expected_loss(us, "reported", "expected", apriori = 1)
u <- unpaid(ec@ultimate)
cat("expected claims", comma(sum(ec@ultimate)), "(book 569,281,839)\n")
cat("IBNR ", comma(u[1]), " (book 25,800,252), total unpaid ", comma(u[2]), " (book 71,231,471)\n", sep = "")
cat("IBNR 2000: ", comma(ec@reserve[3]), " (book -3,156,946)\n", sep = "")
```

```text
expected claims 569,281,839 (book 569,281,839)
IBNR 25,800,252 (book 25,800,252), total unpaid 71,231,471 (book 71,231,471)
IBNR 2000: -3,156,946 (book -3,156,946)
```

For XYZ the selected ratios, the result of the book's adjustments for trend,
rate level and tort reform, are taken as printed in Exhibit III, sheet 1,
column (11):

```{r}
#| label: xyz-ec
XYZ_RATIO <- c(rep(0.783, 6), 0.871, 0.783, 0.658, 0.638, 0.825)
xyz <- make_triangle(XYZ_YEARS, list(reported = XYZ_REPORTED, paid = XYZ_PAID),
                     list(premium = XYZ_PREMIUM, expected = XYZ_RATIO * XYZ_PREMIUM),
                     first_age = XYZ_FIRST_AGE)
xec <- expected_loss(xyz, "reported", "expected", apriori = 1)
u <- unpaid(xec@ultimate, xyz)
cat("expected claims", comma(sum(xec@ultimate)), "(book 561,516)\n")
cat("IBNR ", comma(u[1]), " (book 111,890), total unpaid ", comma(u[2]), " (book 230,887)\n", sep = "")
```

```text
expected claims 561,516 (book 561,516)
IBNR 111,890 (book 111,890), total unpaid 230,889 (book 230,887)
```

The total unpaid is 2 above the book's because it subtracts paid claims: the
book's paid total is 330,629, while its eleven printed paid values add to
330,627, the clearest evidence that the exhibits print rounded data.

## 4. The Bornhuetter-Ferguson technique (chapter 9)

Claims to date plus expected claims times `1 - 1 / CDF`, with the expected
claims of chapter 8 and the rounded CDFs of chapter 7 (chapter 9, Exhibit I):

```{r}
#| label: bf
BOOK_BF_US <- list(  # chapter 9, Exhibit I, sheet 1, columns (11) and (12)
  reported = c(47742304, 51185767, 54889558, 56462300, 58947116,
               58178105, 58317678, 59754938, 60778247, 62835336),
  paid = c(47746843, 51205350, 54841461, 56470405, 58972346,
           58096743, 58447423, 60151912, 61425942, 63209774)
)
bf <- lapply(c(reported = "reported", paid = "paid"), function(col) {
  bornhuetter_ferguson(us, col, "expected", apriori = 1, ldf = US_CDF[[col]], ldf_kind = "cdf")
})
compare(US_YEARS, list(reported = list(bf$reported@ultimate, BOOK_BF_US$reported, 569091348),
                       paid = list(bf$paid@ultimate, BOOK_BF_US$paid, 570568198)), width = 11)
show_unpaid("reported", bf$reported@ultimate, c(25609761, 71040980))
show_unpaid("paid", bf$paid@ultimate, c(27086611, 72517830))
```

## 5. The Benktander technique (chapter 9)

Benktander runs Bornhuetter-Ferguson twice, the first BF ultimate serving as
the expected claims of the second. The book shows it only on synthetic
scenarios (chapter 9, Exhibits V and VI). Its formula, reported claims plus the
BF ultimate times the percentage unreported, fed with the printed U.S. BF
ultimates, checks `benktander(n_iters = 2)`:

```{r}
#| label: benktander
gb <- benktander(us, "reported", "expected", apriori = 1, n_iters = 2,
                 ldf = US_CDF$reported, ldf_kind = "cdf")
cdf_by_year <- rev(CDF_REPORTED)  # the oldest year has the oldest age
by_hand <- latest(us, "reported") + (1 - 1 / cdf_by_year) * BOOK_BF_US$reported
cat(sprintf("%4s %11s %11s %11s %11s\n", "year", "prospicio", "formula", "dev", "BF"))
for (i in seq_along(US_YEARS)) {
  cat(sprintf("%4d %s %s %s %s\n", US_YEARS[i], comma(gb@ultimate[i], 11), comma(by_hand[i], 11),
              comma(BOOK_DEV$reported[i], 11), comma(BOOK_BF_US$reported[i], 11)))
}
cat("largest difference under 0.5:", max(abs(gb@ultimate - by_hand)) < 0.5, "\n")
```

```text

largest difference under 0.5: TRUE
```

Each Benktander ultimate lies between the BF and the development ultimates,
closer to development where the year is mature.

## 6. The Cape Cod technique (chapter 10)

Cape Cod estimates the expected claim ratio from the data: reported claims over
used-up premium. For U.S. Industry Auto (chapter 10, Exhibit I):

```{r}
#| label: cc
cc <- cape_cod(us, "reported", "premium", ldf = US_CDF$reported, ldf_kind = "cdf")
cat(sprintf("expected claim ratio %.5f (book prints 69.5%%)\n", cc@apriori[1]))
cat("ultimate", comma(sum(cc@ultimate)), "(book 570,800,677)\n")
u <- unpaid(cc@ultimate)
cat("IBNR ", comma(u[1]), " (book 27,319,090), total unpaid ", comma(u[2]), " (book 72,750,309)\n", sep = "")
flat <- bornhuetter_ferguson(us, "reported", "premium", apriori = 0.695,
                             ldf = US_CDF$reported, ldf_kind = "cdf")
cat("BF at exactly 69.5%: ultimate", comma(sum(flat@ultimate)), "\n")
```

```text
expected claim ratio 0.69544 (book prints 69.5%)
ultimate 570,800,677 (book 570,800,677)
IBNR 27,319,090 (book 27,319,090), total unpaid 72,750,309 (book 72,750,309)
BF at exactly 69.5%: ultimate 570,783,246
```

The ratio the book prints as 69.5% is 69.544% in its spreadsheet. For XYZ
(chapter 10, Exhibit II) the book puts every year on the 2008 basis: on-level
premium, claims trended at 3.425% a year and adjusted for tort reform. The
ratio is estimated on the adjusted claims with `cape_cod(trend = 0.03425)`, and
its expected claims then go into a BF fit on the actual claims:

```{r}
#| label: xyz-cc
ON_LEVEL_PREMIUM <- c(19783, 30548, 42784, 46606, 55911, 60204, 80411, 97258, 68850, 49950, 47797)
TORT <- c(rep(0.670, 8), 0.750, 1.000, 1.000)
adjusted <- Map(function(row, t) row * t, XYZ_REPORTED, TORT)
xyz_cc <- make_triangle(XYZ_YEARS, list(adjusted = adjusted, reported = XYZ_REPORTED),
                        list(on_level = ON_LEVEL_PREMIUM), first_age = XYZ_FIRST_AGE)
ratio <- cape_cod(xyz_cc, "adjusted", "on_level", trend = 0.03425,
                  ldf = XYZ_CDF$reported, ldf_kind = "cdf")
cat(sprintf("adjusted expected claim ratio %.4f (book 70.8%%)\n", ratio@apriori[length(XYZ_YEARS)]))
cc_expected <- ratio@apriori * ON_LEVEL_PREMIUM / TORT
xyz_cc <- make_triangle(XYZ_YEARS, list(reported = XYZ_REPORTED), list(cc_expected = cc_expected),
                        first_age = XYZ_FIRST_AGE)
xcc <- bornhuetter_ferguson(xyz_cc, "reported", "cc_expected", apriori = 1,
                            ldf = XYZ_CDF$reported, ldf_kind = "cdf")
cat("unadjusted ratios", f3(cc_expected / XYZ_PREMIUM), "\n")
BOOK_CC_XYZ <- c(15822, 25107, 37246, 38798, 48313, 45062, 74754, 77931, 58759, 43307, 39201)
compare(XYZ_YEARS, list("Cape Cod" = list(xcc@ultimate, BOOK_CC_XYZ, 504300)))
```

```text
adjusted expected claim ratio 0.7078 (book 70.8%)
unadjusted ratios 0.746 0.757 0.767 0.778 0.789 0.777 0.747 0.672 0.565 0.547 0.708
year Cape Cod     book
1998   15,822   15,822
1999   25,107   25,107
2000   37,246   37,246
2001   38,798   38,798
2002   48,313   48,313
2003   45,063   45,062
2004   74,754   74,754
2005   77,931   77,931
2006   58,759   58,759
2007   43,307   43,307
2008   39,201   39,201

```

The adjusted ratio, the unadjusted ratios by year (the book's column (15)) and
the total of 504,300 agree; 2003 is 1 above, the rounding of the printed data.
The tort factor multiplies the claims rather than dividing the premium, since
the ratio is a ratio of sums.

## 7. Reasonableness checks (chapters 8 and 15)

Chapter 15 summarizes U.S. Industry Auto's unpaid claims by method in billions
of dollars:

```{r}
#| label: summary
book_billions <- list(  # chapter 15, IBNR and total unpaid, $ billions
  "Development, reported" = c(26, 71), "Development, paid" = c(29, 74),
  "Expected claims" = c(26, 71), "B-F, reported" = c(26, 71),
  "B-F, paid" = c(27, 73), "Cape Cod" = c(27, 73)
)
fits <- list(dev_r, dev_p, ec, bf$reported, bf$paid, cc)
cat(sprintf("%-22s %5s %5s %6s %5s\n", "method", "IBNR", "book", "total", "book"))
for (i in seq_along(fits)) {
  u <- unpaid(fits[[i]]@ultimate) / 1e6
  b <- book_billions[[i]]
  cat(sprintf("%-22s %5.0f %5d %6.0f %5d\n", names(book_billions)[i], u[1], b[1], u[2], b[2]))
}
```

```text
method                  IBNR  book  total  book
Development, reported     26    26     71    71
Development, paid         29    29     74    74
Expected claims           26    26     71    71
B-F, reported             26    26     71    71
B-F, paid                 27    27     73    73
Cape Cod                  27    27     73    73
```

All twelve figures agree (the book's row for the case outstanding development
technique is not reproduced). For XYZ, chapter 8, Exhibit III, sheet 1, column
(10) prints the claim ratio of the average of the two development ultimates;
beside it, the ratio implied by each method:

```{r}
#| label: ratios
BOOK_AVG_RATIO <- c(79.5, 79.8, 83.2, 79.1, 80.0, 68.5, 78.2, 56.8, 60.6, 100.8, 128.2)
methods <- list("dev rep" = xdev_r, "dev paid" = xdev_p, "EC" = xec,
                "BF rep" = xbf$reported, "BF paid" = xbf$paid, "CC" = xcc)
cat("year  avg dev   book", paste(sprintf("%8s", names(methods)), collapse = " "), "\n")
for (i in seq_along(XYZ_YEARS)) {
  avg <- (xdev_r@ultimate[i] + xdev_p@ultimate[i]) / 2 / XYZ_PREMIUM[i]
  each <- vapply(methods, function(f) sprintf("%7.1f%%", 100 * f@ultimate[i] / XYZ_PREMIUM[i]), "")
  cat(sprintf("%4d %7.1f%% %5.1f%%", XYZ_YEARS[i], 100 * avg, BOOK_AVG_RATIO[i]), paste(each, collapse = " "), "\n")
}
```

The average-of-development column equals the book's. The development ratios
for 2007 and 2008 are out of line with every earlier year, while the expected
claims, BF and Cape Cod methods keep them near the history; the book's
conclusion for XYZ rests on Berquist-Sherman adjusted projections, which
prospicio does not make.

## 8. What prospicio does not cover

As in the Python guide: averages over the latest n years, medial and geometric
averages as options of `chain_ladder()` (issue #336; the workarounds are
above), CDFs below 1 as a `"cdf"` pattern (#336), the frequency-severity
techniques (chapter 11), the case outstanding development technique (chapter
12), Berquist-Sherman adjustments (chapter 13), the ALAE and ULAE methods
(chapters 16 and 17) and the trend, rate-level and tort adjustments of the
expected claims method, which are inputs prepared by hand. Every R function
this guide needs exists with the same arguments as its Python counterpart.
